content: The SPICE framework was employed to guide the development of research questions, as it is particularly suited for qualitative and mixed-methods evidence searches, unlike the traditional PICO format. A comprehensive explanation of the SPICE framework is available in Annex 3. Once the SPICE-based questions were finalized, requests for proposals were distributed, and three systematic review teams were engaged: one from Harvard University led by Elena Savoia, another from the University of Central Florida led by Tim Sellnow, and a third from Wayne State University led by Lillian Lee Wilkins. Additionally, Deborah Toppenberg-Pejcic was tasked with conducting reviews based on the formulated questions. Details of the teams are provided in Annex 1. Throughout the process of evidence search, analysis, and reporting, the review teams received guidance and support from Jane Noyes, the WHO risk communication guidelines secretariat, and Tomas Allen, a WHO Information Scientist, who assisted with database and grey literature searches. During this period, significant public health emergencies, such as the West African Ebola virus outbreak and the emergence of Zika virus syndrome, generated a substantial amount of grey literature on risk communication. To capture this, a rapid grey literature evidence search was conducted by Deborah Toppenberg-Pejcic, focusing on reports relevant to the 12 formulated questions, with a cut-off date of December 31, 2016. All reviews were completed and submitted to the WHO secretariat by the end of January 2017 and subsequently shared with all members of the Guideline Development Group (GDG). To ensure transparent, evidence-based recommendations, the review findings were used to adapt the DECIDE Evidence to Decision (EtD) framework tables. These tables summarized evidence on effective and ineffective practices, as well as considerations related to values, preferences, resource use, and equity. An initial anonymous electronic voting system was employed to establish the GDG’s position, after which recommendations were formulated and consensus was reached. The recommendations were compiled and sent to the GDG for further review. This finalized set of recommendations was then included in the guideline document and reviewed by the External Review Group (ERG), which consisted of emergency responders, academics, and policymakers. Their feedback was used to refine the recommendations and the presentation of the guideline document in consultation with the GDG. The 12 priority questions, developed during the first GDG meeting, addressed key areas such as trust, community engagement, integration of emergency risk communication (ERC) into health systems, and evidence-based ERC practices. These questions were further refined into potential search terms using the SPICE framework, with details provided in Annex 3. A scoping flash literature review revealed that most WHO guidance was based on events prior to 2003, so the systematic reviews focused on evidence from 2003 onwards. Due to major public health emergencies like the Ebola and Zika outbreaks, an additional rapid review of recent grey literature covering all 12 questions was commissioned towards the end of the process. Each systematic review team collaborated with Tomas Allen to design and execute extensive searches in research databases in English, other official UN languages (Arabic, Chinese, French, Russian, Spanish), and Portuguese, as well as grey literature. Detailed accounts of these searches are included in the review reports. For each question, the teams mapped the literature and identified gaps using categories such as disaster type, phase, geographical location, income settings, equity considerations, study type, and grey literature. Existing reviews were appraised using the AMSTAR tool to assess methodological quality. Low-quality reviews were unpacked, and their studies were screened for potential inclusion, while mediumto high-quality reviews were used to contextualize findings. Primary studies were appraised using specific tools based on their methodology. Quantitative studies with comparison groups were assessed using the Cochrane EPOC Risk of Bias tool, while descriptive surveys were evaluated using adaptations of existing tools. Qualitative studies were appraised using the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme (CASP), and mixed-methods or case studies were assessed using the McGill Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT). Grey literature was evaluated using the AACODS tool, which considers authority, accuracy, coverage, objectivity, date, and significance. Studies were rated as high, moderate, low, or very low quality based on their methodological rigor. Data extraction focused on study characteristics such as country, disaster type and phase, and whether vulnerable populations were addressed. Evidence relevant to the phenomena of interest and outcomes related to the review questions was identified and extracted. Quantitative studies provided numerical data, while qualitative studies yielded key phrases, sentences, and direct quotations. Mixed-methods and case studies combined these approaches as appropriate. Findings were synthesized within each methodological stream. Quantitative studies were summarized narratively due to the small number of studies with comparison groups and high heterogeneity. For qualitative studies, a framework synthesis model was used, with categories derived from the SPICE questions and modified based on subject knowledge and individual study analysis. Mixed-methods and case studies were also summarized narratively, as they often did not differentiate findings by methodological type. The certainty or confidence in synthesized findings was assessed separately for each methodological stream. Quantitative findings with comparison groups were evaluated using the GRADE approach, while descriptive surveys applied GRADE principles. Qualitative findings were assessed using the GRADE-CERQual tool, which examines methodological limitations, relevance, coherence, and adequacy of data. Mixed-methods and case studies applied both GRADE and GRADE-CERQual principles. Findings were rated as high, moderate, low, or very low confidence based on the likelihood of new evidence altering the conclusions. Synthesized findings across methodological streams were compared and contrasted. When findings supported and amplified each other, they were combined into higher-order findings representing cross-stream syntheses. Subgroup analyses considered factors such as the type and phase of the emergency, country, and the presence of vulnerable populations, enabling equity considerations in the synthesized findings. The results were presented in summary tables with corresponding confidence or certainty assessments.
